Day 51 of 100 · Linux Administration

Linux Networking Tools

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityLinux AdministrationPublished artifact recovered

Linux networking tools become useful when used in an order that proves interfaces, routes, listeners and application reachability instead of as random commands.

Architecture / mental model

interface → route → local socket → network path → application protocol → packet capture

How it works

Start with local state: `ip addr` shows interfaces/addresses and `ip route` shows how the kernel intends to reach a destination. `ss` then answers whether a process is actually listening on the expected address and port.

Connectivity tests should become progressively more specific. Ping can show ICMP reachability where permitted, while `curl` proves an HTTP request/response path rather than merely proving a host exists.

Packet capture with a narrow filter is the final microscope when higher-level tools disagree. It lets you see whether packets leave, return and carry the flags/protocol you expected.

Hands-on reference

ip addr
ip route get 1.1.1.1
ss -lntup
ping -c 3 HOST
curl -v https://example.com
sudo tcpdump -ni any host HOST

Verification

Choose one real service and trace it in order from local interface through route, listening socket and application request. Record the observation at each layer.

Field note / gotcha

A successful ping does not prove the application port is open, and a failed ping does not prove the application is unreachable because ICMP may be filtered.

Security considerations

Packet captures can contain credentials or sensitive payload metadata. Filter tightly, protect capture files and remove them when no longer needed.

What I learned

Prove one layer, then move to the next.
